---
title: "Does Age Slow Down Ultramarathon Runners?"
subtitle: "A worked example of left_join() and case_when()"
author: "Esra Dogan"
format: html
---

## Introduction

Ultramarathons are races longer than a marathon, often around 100 miles through mountains. A natural question is: **does age slow runners down?**

Answering this is harder than it looks. If we only compare finish times by age, we might be comparing an untrained 22-year-old with a 50-year-old who has been racing for decades. We would also ignore everyone who started a race but did not finish. So in this vignette I look at age together with **experience** and **finish rates**.

This vignette focuses on two `dplyr` functions:

- **`left_join()`**, to combine information stored in two separate tables.
- **`case_when()`**, to turn numeric variables (age, number of races) into meaningful groups.

Other familiar functions such as `filter()`, `mutate()`, and `summarise()` appear along the way without detailed explanation.

## The data

The data comes from the [TidyTuesday project](https://github.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/tree/main/data/2021/2021-10-26) (originally from the International Trail Running Association). `read_csv()` can read a file directly from a URL, so nothing needs to be downloaded.

```{r}
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)

rankings <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2021/2021-10-26/ultra_rankings.csv")

races <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2021/2021-10-26/race.csv")
```

There are two tables, and neither is enough on its own:

- `rankings` is the results list: one row per runner per race, with age, gender, nationality, and finish time. It does not say how long the race was.
- `races` is the race catalog: one row per race, with distance, elevation, country, and date. It does not say who ran.

Race details are stored once in `races` instead of being repeated on every runner's row. The two tables are linked by `race_year_id`.

```{r}
glimpse(rankings)
glimpse(races)
```

## Combining the tables with `left_join()`

To compare runners across races of different lengths, I need each race's distance. But distance is stored in `races`, not in `rankings`. Both tables share the column `race_year_id`, so I can use it as a key.

`left_join()` keeps every row of the left table (`rankings`) and adds the matching columns from the right table (`races`). If a race had no match, the new columns would be `NA`, but no runner rows would be lost.

```{r}
ultra <- rankings |>
  left_join(races, by = "race_year_id")

nrow(rankings)
nrow(ultra)
```

The row count is unchanged, which confirms the join added columns without duplicating or dropping runners.

### Checking the join

Before trusting a join, it is worth checking two things. First, the key should be unique in the right table. If a race appeared twice in `races`, each of its runners would be duplicated.

```{r}
races |>
  count(race_year_id) |>
  filter(n > 1)
```

Zero rows means every race appears exactly once. Second, every runner row should find a matching race. `anti_join()` returns the rows of the left table that have **no** match in the right table.

```{r}
rankings |>
  anti_join(races, by = "race_year_id") |>
  nrow()
```

The result is 0, so every result is linked to a race.

## Cleaning the data

First I add two columns with `mutate()`:

- `finished`: `TRUE` if the runner has a finish time. Runners without a time did not finish (DNF), and keeping them lets us study finish rates instead of looking only at "survivors."
- `pace`: minutes per kilometer, so that races of slightly different lengths can be compared.

```{r}
ultra <- ultra |>
  mutate(
    finished = !is.na(time_in_seconds),
    pace = time_in_seconds / 60 / distance
  )
```

The data also has some obvious errors: ages of 0 or 133, races with a distance of 0, and a "runner" named *NO Participants* who covered 168 km in one hour. I keep only:

- ages between 18 and 80,
- races of at least 150 km (these are meant to be 100-mile races, about 161 km),
- paces of at least 4 minutes per km. Anything faster would beat the 100-mile world record, so it must be a data error. Runners who did not finish have no pace (`NA`) and are kept.

```{r}
ultra_clean <- ultra |>
  filter(
    age >= 18, age <= 80,
    distance >= 150,
    is.na(pace) | pace >= 4
  )

nrow(ultra)
nrow(ultra_clean)
```

About 10,500 rows are removed, most of them from races with a recorded distance of 0.

Note the condition `is.na(pace) | pace >= 4`. Without the `is.na(pace)` part, `filter()` would silently drop every runner who did not finish, because `NA >= 4` is `NA`, and `filter()` keeps only rows where the condition is `TRUE`.

## Measuring experience with `add_count()`

The data has no "experience" column, but it can be built. Each row is one runner in one race, so a runner who raced five times appears in five rows. `add_count()` counts how often each runner appears and adds the result as a new column, without collapsing the rows the way `count()` would.

Runners are identified by name, gender, and nationality together. This reduces, but does not eliminate, the chance that two different people with the same name are counted as one runner.

```{r}
ultra_clean <- ultra_clean |>
  add_count(runner, gender, nationality, name = "n_races")
```

This is only an approximation: it counts races in this dataset, not a runner's whole career.

## Creating groups with `case_when()`

Age and number of races are numbers, but for comparison it is easier to work with groups. `case_when()` is a vectorized "if / else if" statement. Each line has the form `condition ~ value`.

```{r}
ultra_clean <- ultra_clean |>
  mutate(
    age_group = case_when(
      age < 30 ~ "18-29",
      age < 40 ~ "30-39",
      age < 50 ~ "40-49",
      age < 60 ~ "50-59",
      age >= 60 ~ "60+"
    ),
    experience = case_when(
      n_races == 1 ~ "1 race",
      n_races <= 4 ~ "2-4 races",
      n_races >= 5 ~ "5+ races"
    )
  )
```

Two things are worth knowing about `case_when()`:

1. **Order matters.** Conditions are checked from top to bottom, and each row gets the value of the *first* condition that is true. That is why the second line can simply say `age < 40`: anyone under 30 was already caught by the first line.
2. **Unmatched rows become `NA`.** If a row meets none of the conditions, it gets `NA`, so it is good practice to check the result.

```{r}
ultra_clean |> count(age_group)
ultra_clean |> count(experience)
```

There are no `NA` groups, so every row was matched. Most ultramarathon runners are in their 40s and 50s. Runners under 30 are a small minority.

## Does age matter?

### Finish rate by age

First, how often do runners in each age group finish the race?

```{r}
by_age <- ultra_clean |>
  group_by(age_group) |>
  summarise(
    runners = n(),
    finish_rate = mean(finished),
    median_pace = median(pace, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

by_age
```

```{r}
by_age |>
  ggplot(aes(x = age_group, y = finish_rate)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#0072B2", width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::percent(finish_rate, accuracy = 1)), vjust = -0.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Older runners do not drop out more often",
    subtitle = "Share of runners who finished the race, by age group",
    x = "Age group",
    y = "Finish rate"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))
```

Finish rates do not fall with age. The **youngest** runners are actually the least likely to finish (about 77%), while runners in their 40s and 50s finish about 88% of the time. Older runners are slower when they finish: the median pace goes from about 10.9 minutes per km for the youngest group to about 12.4 for runners over 60. But they are not more likely to drop out.

### Finish rate by experience

Now the same question for experience instead of age.

```{r}
by_exp <- ultra_clean |>
  group_by(experience) |>
  summarise(
    runners = n(),
    finish_rate = mean(finished),
    median_pace = median(pace, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

by_exp
```

```{r}
by_exp |>
  ggplot(aes(x = experience, y = finish_rate)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#D55E00", width = 0.5) +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::percent(finish_rate, accuracy = 1)), vjust = -0.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "More experienced runners finish more often",
    subtitle = "Share of runners who finished the race, by number of races in the dataset",
    x = "Experience",
    y = "Finish rate"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))
```

Here the pattern is clear and goes in one direction: the finish rate rises from about 83% for runners with a single race to about 93% for runners with five or more. Experienced runners are also faster, with a median pace of about 10.7 minutes per km compared with 12.7 for first-timers.

### Age and experience together

Finally, the table below splits each experience level by age group. It compares runners of different ages who have raced a similar number of times.

```{r}
ultra_clean |>
  group_by(experience, age_group) |>
  summarise(
    runners = n(),
    finish_rate = mean(finished),
    median_pace = median(pace, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

Within every experience level, pace still slows with age, so age does have an effect on speed. But runners with five or more races finish more than 90% of the time at every age, and runners over 60 in that group are about as fast as first-time runners under 30 (about 11.3 vs. 11.4 minutes per km).

## Conclusion

Age does slow ultramarathon runners down, but less than a simple comparison suggests, and experience appears to matter more. Younger runners are faster when they finish, but they are also the most likely to drop out.

Some limits to keep in mind:

- "Experience" counts races in this dataset only, and includes races that happened *after* the one in each row.
- Runners are matched by name, gender, and nationality, which is not a perfect identifier.
- People who race many times are probably not a random group. They may be the runners who were already good at this, so experience and talent are mixed together.

In terms of the tidyverse, `left_join()` made the analysis possible by bringing race distance into the results table, and `case_when()` turned raw numbers into the groups that the comparison is built on.
